title: Estrogen-Only Therapy May Not Raise Dementia Risk, Major Review Finds
excerpt: A WHO-commissioned meta-analysis of more than one million women found menopause hormone therapy neither increases nor decreases dementia risk, while a separate study suggests estrogen-only treatment may be safer than combined therapy.
body:
• A WHO-commissioned meta-analysis published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity found no evidence that menopause hormone therapy (MHT) increases or decreases dementia risk
  • A separate JAMA study found estrogen-only therapy did not amplify dementia risk in women with high Alzheimer's biomarker levels, unlike combined hormone therapy
  • The FDA removed "black box" dementia warnings from hormone therapy products in late 2025
  • Experts say decisions about MHT should focus on symptom relief and quality of life, not fear of cognitive decline

Landmark Review Challenges Decades of Concern

For more than two decades, fears about a link between menopause hormone therapy and dementia have shaped prescribing patterns and patient decisions worldwide. A new body of research is pushing back against those fears with data from over a million women.

The WHO-commissioned meta-analysis, published in The Lancet Healthy Longevity, reviewed ten studies and found that MHT — used to treat symptoms like hot flushes, night sweats, and mood disturbances — neither increased nor decreased dementia risk in postmenopausal women.

"Dementia should not drive MHT decisions."

— Melissa Melville, PhD Candidate, University College London

"The World Health Organisation currently provides no guidance on MHT and dementia risk, leaving a critical gap for women, clinicians, and policymakers. Our work will help inform upcoming WHO guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia," said Melissa Melville, an aging researcher at University College London and the study's lead author, according to Healthline.

Estrogen-Only Shows Distinct Pattern

While the meta-analysis looked at hormone therapy broadly, a separate study published in JAMA added nuance by examining how different types of therapy interact with Alzheimer's biomarkers.

Researchers analyzed blood samples from 2,766 women recruited into a clinical trial between 1996 and 1999, following them until 2021. They measured levels of plasma p-tau217, a biomarker linked to brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Among women assigned to combined hormone therapy — containing both estrogen and progesterone — higher biomarker levels were linked to roughly four times the risk of developing dementia. But this pattern was not observed among women using estrogen-only therapy, typically prescribed after hysterectomy, according to an analysis by Loughborough University.

The finding suggests estrogen-only therapy may be a safer option for women with elevated Alzheimer's biomarkers, though researchers caution that more study is needed.

Undoing the WHI's Shadow

The roots of the dementia fear trace back to 2002, when the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study (WHIMS) — the only large randomized controlled trial of MHT — found that estrogen plus progestin doubled the risk of dementia in women aged 65 and older. That single finding had an outsized and decades-long impact on clinical practice.

"A lot of other research was halted at that point, which led to only really having this study as our data point for many years," said Dr. Caroline Just, program lead for women's neurology at the Cleveland Clinic, in an interview with Healthline.

Experts note that the WHI used hormone formulations and patient populations — women over 65 — that differ substantially from current clinical practice.

"It is not reflective of our practice patterns now, nor the hormone therapy regimens that we use now," said Dr. Karen Adams, director of the Stanford Program in Menopause & Healthy Aging at Stanford Medicine.

Regulatory Shift Follows the Data

In November 2025, the FDA removed its most stringent "black box" warnings from menopause hormone therapy products. Those warnings had cited potential complications including cardiovascular disease, cancer, and dementia.

The new findings add to a growing body of evidence that some of those concerns were overstated, particularly regarding cognitive outcomes.

What Women Should Know

For women under 60 or within 10 years of their last menstrual period, experts say there is a window to start MHT with limited risk. "To the best of our knowledge, if you start at the right time, you can continue indefinitely without significant risk," Adams said.

The best evidence for reducing dementia risk still points to lifestyle factors: regular physical activity, a heart-healthy diet such as the Mediterranean diet, not smoking, maintaining healthy blood pressure and cholesterol, staying socially active, and prioritizing sleep.

"We just don't have good studies. The best thing we can say right now is that hormone therapy probably does not increase the risk of dementia, but it probably doesn't prevent it either."

— Dr. Karen Adams, Stanford Medicine

"Many cases of dementia are likely modifiable, meaning there's something that the patients can do to alter or reduce their risk that is not genetic," Just said.

Women disproportionately bear the burden of dementia, making up roughly two-thirds of Americans living with Alzheimer's disease even after accounting for longer life expectancy. The apparently neutral effect of MHT on dementia risk suggests one clear takeaway: decisions about using the therapy should be guided by symptom relief and quality of life, not fear.
